growth_story.headline: Australia's income per person grew steadily for three decades, but growth slowed to 0.8 percent a year in 2016-2025 and income is below its 2023 peak.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, income per person in Australia has grown by an average of 1.5 percent a year, and the data show no lasting break in that pace from 1990 to 2025. Within that single era, growth has eased. It ran between 2.6 and 3.9 percent a year from 1993 to 1999, then averaged 1.1 percent over 2006-2015 and 0.8 percent over 2016-2025. The OECD links the strong late 1990s to productivity gains from competition reforms and dates the productivity slowdown to the mid-2000s. Falls were rare and short: income per person dropped in 1991 and 1992, was flat in 2009 (-0.1), and fell 1.4 percent in 2020 before rising 1.9 and 2.9 percent in 2021 and 2022. It peaked in 2023, then fell in 2024 (-0.6) and 2025 (-0.2) to 0.8 percent below that peak, as higher prices and tighter money squeezed household incomes while the population grew fast after the pandemic.

threads.title: A long productivity slowdown
threads.text: Both the IMF and the OECD describe productivity growth that has been weak for years. The OECD says the slowdown began in the mid-2000s. The IMF links it to slow uptake of new technology, fading business dynamism and capital that is slow to move to better uses, which fits the drift in income per person growth from 1.1 percent a year over 2006-2015 to 0.8 percent over 2016-2025.

threads.title: Competition reforms of the 1990s
threads.text: The OECD says the National Competition Policy, agreed by all governments in 1995 and wound up in 2006, helped productivity growth strengthen in the late 1990s and early 2000s. In the data, income per person grew between 2.6 and 3.9 percent a year from 1993 to 1999, well above the 1.5 percent average since 1990.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Australia 2026
citations.quote: Productivity growth strengthened notably during the late 1990s and early 2000s, with competition reforms cited as a key contributor.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Australia 2026
citations.quote: the Commonwealth, states and territories entered into three intergovernmental agreements in 1995 to implement the National Competition Policy (NCP).

threads.title: Mining boom and its aftermath
threads.text: By 2016 the IMF described Australia as moving out of a mining boom. Mining still has an outsized effect on measured productivity. The OECD notes that output per mine tends to fall as the easiest deposits run out, and it names mining as one reason productivity growth before the pandemic was about half its long-run average.

threads.title: Population surge after the pandemic
threads.text: After the pandemic, a surge in immigration made the population grow fast. The OECD says real consumption was flat from early 2022 to late 2024 as household incomes fell sharply, and income per person fell in 2024 and 2025. The IMF reports that migration eased from those peaks during 2025.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Australia 2026
citations.quote: Real aggregate consumption was broadly flat between early 2022 and late 2024, despite rapid growth of the population driven by a surge in immigration

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Australia 2026
citations.quote: The softness of consumption growth largely reflected a sharp fall in real disposable household income

threads.title: Steady growth, rare recessions
threads.text: Australia has long had few recessions, and its growth has varied little from year to year. The OECD notes that 2020 was the first year output fell since 1991. In the data, before 2024 income per person fell only in 1991, 1992 and 2020, and was flat in 2009 (-0.1).

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Australia 2026
citations.quote: resilience during the shocks of the past half-decade fits with its long-term experience of low variance of GDP growth and avoidance of recessions

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Australia 2026
citations.quote: its first year of negative GDP growth since 1991 followed by its fastest annual growth since 1984 and then another sharp slowdown

since_last_year.text: In February 2026, the IMF reported that during 2025 the economy recovered from a weak 2024 as private demand picked up and interest rates were cut. In January 2026, the OECD described the economy as recovering towards its trend path. The annual data do not yet show this in income per person, which fell 0.2 percent in 2025.

citations.title: Australia: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Alternate Executive Director for Australia (IMF Country Report No. 26/38)
citations.quote: Growth picked up to 2.1 percent year on year in 2025Q3 after a weak 2024, as private demand gradually recovered.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Australia 2026
citations.quote: the economy is now recovering towards its trend path

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes a soft landing, the OECD an economy now recovering, and total output kept growing through the slowdown. Yet income per person fell in 2024 and 2025 and is 0.8 percent below its 2023 peak, because the population grew faster than output after the pandemic.
